source: Modelled on NASA's Mars 2020 Perseverance mission (NASA Mars 2020 mission pages and launch press kit: landing in Jezero crater at 18.4 N 77.5 E, entry at about 5.4 km/s, sky-crane powered descent, relay through Mars orbiters, coring of rock samples) and Mars Science Laboratory mass breakdown (3,893 kg at launch for an 899 kg rover: aeroshell, parachute, descent and cruise stages make up the rest). Launch and arrival dates use the 2028 Earth-Mars window computed from JPL Keplerian elements. Dust accumulation of about 0.2 % per sol follows Mars Exploration Rover experience. Site science values, distances and hazard factors are simplified for gameplay.
units: Same fields as the lunar scenario. route: the launch window for a ballistic Earth-Mars transfer whose launch energy and arrival speed follow from the chosen dates (landing_window bounds the arrival). entry: mass_fraction is the heat shield, parachute and cruise stage as a share of the fuelled lander mass; max_entry_speed_m_s the fastest atmospheric entry the heat shield survives; interface_altitude_m where the atmosphere begins. descent.delta_v_m_s is the powered descent after the parachute. sky: diurnal = Sun and Earth rise and set each sol; equinox_longitude_deg is the heliocentric ecliptic longitude of Mars at northern spring equinox; conjunction_elongation_deg the Sun-Earth angle below which the Sun drowns the radio link. sites: horizon masks are unused by the diurnal sky (flat horizon); ice_quality is the richness of the rock record; shadow_distance_km the drive from the landing zone to the rocks worth coring.
name: Jezero crater sample survey
tagline: Core the rocks of a vanished Martian lake.
briefing: Three and a half billion years ago a river filled Jezero crater and built a delta on its floor. If Mars ever had life, mud like that is where its traces would be kept. Send a rover across 200 million kilometres, land it beside the delta, and core the rocks that record the water. Mars is only in reach every 26 months: pick your launch and arrival dates from the porkchop plot, bring power that survives dust and cold nights, and remember that every command takes many minutes to arrive.

route.name: Interplanetary transfer
route.summary: A coasting arc around the Sun. The launch date and the arrival date together fix how hard the rocket must push and how fast the spacecraft meets Mars.

terms.find_detail: of rock laid down in water was sealed in its tube
terms.empty_sample: were of rock that never saw water
terms.find_advice: A site with a richer rock record makes more of the cores count.

descent.summary: Heat shield, parachute, then a powered descent for the last two kilometres.

sites.name: Crater floor
sites.summary: Flat volcanic plains east of the delta: the safest touchdown and rocks within a short drive, but they are lava, and only some of them were ever soaked by the lake.

sites.name: Delta front
sites.summary: Right under the delta cliffs, where Perseverance was aimed. The mudstones are a short climb away; the landing zone is full of boulders, dunes and scarps.

sites.name: Western rim
sites.summary: High ground where the river cut through the crater wall. The oldest and most varied rocks in Jezero, at the end of a long drive over steep slopes.

objectives.name: Core rocks that record the lake
objectives.summary: Drill cores from water-laid rock and check them for the minerals and organic molecules water leaves behind.

objectives.name: Survey the route with cameras
objectives.summary: Drive and image as you go: the context that tells scientists where each core came from.

objectives.name: Return the data to Earth
objectives.summary: Science only counts once it is on the ground, and Mars is a long way to shout.

objectives.name: Characterise the site
objectives.summary: Each extra kind of measurement (chemistry, buried layers, weather) tells the next mission what to expect.

reference_design.name: Solar rover baseline
reference_design.summary: A solar rover with a deck array, a coring drill and a Raman spectrometer, landing on the crater floor with terrain-relative navigation and talking through the orbiters.

nasa_reference.summary: NASA sent Perseverance to Jezero for exactly this: a one-tonne rover that cores rock, seals the samples in tubes and leaves them for a later mission to bring home. It runs on a radioisotope generator, so dust storms and winter do not stop it; it landed within metres of its target using terrain-relative navigation and a sky crane; and it sends almost all of its data through orbiters overhead rather than straight to Earth.
